name: Priya Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for having me. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say is confidential. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Gabor and I run Elm Tree Farm, 45 hectares with 80 milking goats, oats and a big vegetable patch. I milk at six, make cheese three mornings a week, and the afternoons go on the veg box scheme, which delivers to about 140 households in town. Before any of that, I talk to the computer every morning before I talk to the goats, and the goats don't mind.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you use the computer for?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: An AI assistant sorts the box orders, writes the weekly newsletter draft and plans the crop rotation with me. It saves me two hours a day, easily. The worry is money: we borrowed for the new goat parlour, so we've less than a month's cushion, and the income's modest for all the hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Oh, I'd be a bit disappointed, to be honest. I like my little helper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the other box scheme farmers that even modest AI is worth having, and I'd show them how I use it. Online I'd say the hype was overblown but the tools are still useful for small farms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, a tool that books my deliveries is the most exciting thing to happen to this farm since we bought the goats. But it doesn't fix the loan. Our real pressure is the parlour repayments and a thin bank balance, and that stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move the last of the box orders onto the AI ordering assistant this spring, so Gabor stops doing them on paper. And I'd keep milking 80 goats and making cheese three days a week. Nothing else would change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. A bit restless, because I like things to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the two hours you save?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd sleep. Or I'd make the halloumi-style cheese I've been meaning to try, because it sells better at the market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the loan a big worry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's always there. One bad kidding season and we're borrowing from my sister. But the cheese sells, so I don't lie awake.

The hype was overblown, but I'd still **show other farmers** how I use it.
think: A delivery-booking tool is **exciting** for a farm like ours.
The **parlour loan** and thin savings are the real pressure, and they stay.
do: Move the last **box orders** onto the AI assistant this spring.
**Keep milking** 80 goats and making cheese three days a week.

She shares tools with **other farmers**, a cooperative instinct.

steps.text: Move the last box scheme orders onto the AI assistant this spring

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one feels close to where we're already heading.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say small farms that learn these tools early can beat the big ones on service. I'd also say loudly that governments should pay for training so older farmers aren't left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's good for me. My day is mostly hands-on, and the thinking bits, like ordering and newsletters, are already done with AI. A weeding robot is too dear for one small farm, but four farms sharing one is a co-op, and co-ops are how farmers have always survived.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take an online course on AI for small food businesses this winter, maybe ten evenings. Then I'd go round to the three farms near us and set up a shared weeding robot, splitting the cost four ways. I'd want it running by next summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, with a little nag at the back about the big box companies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the nag?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big national box companies would get AI too, and they've got more money. If they cut their prices, my 140 households might drift away to them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your partner Gabor: how does he feel about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gabor is happy with paper and a pencil, bless him. He'll grumble about the robot for a month and then name it.

Governments should **pay for training** so older farmers keep up.
think: My **thinking work** is already done with AI, so this mostly helps me.
Four farms sharing one **weeding robot** is how farmers survive.
do: Take a ten-evening **online course** on AI for small food businesses this winter.
Set up a **shared weeding robot** with three neighbouring farms by next summer.
feel: **Excited**, with a nag about big box companies cutting prices.
S1.quote: A weeding robot is too dear for one small farm, but four farms sharing one is a co-op, and co-ops are how farmers have always survived.
fieldNote: Her hands-on work is **safe** in this picture; AI already handles her admin.
Sees **cooperation** as the answer to costly robots.
The quiet risk is **big competitors** using the same tools with deeper pockets.

steps.text: Take a ten-evening online course on AI for small food businesses

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Oh. Now that's different. That frightens me, and not for the reason you'd think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say publicly that we need public money for farm co-ops to share robots, fast, or only the big players will have them. I'd say it at every meeting I could get to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, my cheese customers are the people with office jobs, so when AGI takes their jobs in 2028, my goat cheese becomes a luxury nobody can afford. The robots don't reach my goats until 2031, but my customers are gone by 2029. That's the gap that scares me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month, I'd cut the herd from 80 to 50 goats to cut feed bills. I'd start running weekend cheese-making courses, because people who've lost office jobs will want hands-on skills. And I'd campaign hard for public money for farm co-ops to buy robots together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, then busy. I'm the sort who copes by making lists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you sell to, if the office workers can't afford you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, and that's honest. Maybe the people who still have money, maybe a shop in the city. I'd have to find out fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Selling 30 goats: how does that feel for someone who loves them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Awful. I know every one by name, and Pepper, the old lead goat, would stay whatever happens. But you can't feed goats on love when the boxes stop selling.

Otherwise only the **big players** will own the machines.
think: My customers are **office workers**, and AGI hits them in 2028.
Sales fall **before the robots** reach my goats in 2031.

fieldNote: Sharp insight: her risk comes through **customers' jobs**, not her own hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That I can work with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time for co-ops, and I'd be on the phone to every goat farmer in the region. I'd post about it every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough time to change who I sell to, if I start the week the warning comes. I'd be 63 when AGI arrives and 66 when the robots do. So I'd want the farm in shape to hand on, not just to survive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay off the parlour loan two years early by putting every spare bit of cheese money into it. I'd form a goat dairy co-op with four farms to share a robot milker and sell cheese to city shops under one label. And I'd move my AI tools from orders to wholesale pricing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, mostly. Nervous about the customer side, but there's time to change it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Paying off the loan early leaves you with no cushion at all. Is that wise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe not. But the loan is what makes a bad year dangerous, and I'd rather owe nothing when the robots come. Gabor thinks I'm mad, and he might be right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your own children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marek tests software for a living, so he'd be hit by the thinking AI. I'd tell Marek to come and learn cheese with me for a year before the robots arrive, just in case.

say: This is the time for **co-ops** across the region.
I'll be on the phone to every **goat farmer** I know.
think: Five years is enough to change **who I sell to**, if I start now.
I'd want the farm **ready to hand on**, not just surviving.
do: Pay off the **parlour loan** two years early from cheese money.

S3.quote: Five years is enough time to change who I sell to, if I start the week the warning comes.
fieldNote: Treats five years as **planning time** and moves straight to action.

steps.text: Pay off the goat parlour loan two years early

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be retired before the robots, surely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've no excuse this time; governments and farmers have a decade. I'd push the co-op idea, but calmly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd rather hand Elm Tree Farm to a young couple with robots than to an investor with a spreadsheet. AGI in 2036 means I'd be 68 and probably handing over. My money's still thin, so the sale price matters a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running the box scheme with AI help as long as it sells. From about 2032 I'd look for a young couple through the farm starter scheme to take over the farm, with a slow handover over two years. That way the herd stays together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm-ish. A bit sad about stopping, but the goats would be in good hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not pass the farm to your own children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Neither Marek nor Lena wants it, and I won't guilt them into it. Lena loves animals, but she's a vet nurse in the city and happy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the sale give you enough to retire on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Land here isn't worth much, and the parlour's half paid. We'd live small, and that's fine.

I'd still push the **co-op idea**, but more calmly.
think: I'd rather sell to a **young couple** than to an investor.
My savings are **thin**, so the sale price really matters.
do: **Keep running** the box scheme with AI help as long as it sells.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my customers lose their jobs before my goats ever see a robot. What would help is public money for farm co-ops to share robots, and some kind of income support for the town, so people can still buy real food.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether farmers like the tools. I do, and people assume a 58-year-old woman with goats won't. That's half the problem.

headlineQuote: I talk to the computer every morning before I talk to the goats, and the goats don't mind.
portrait: Priya, 58, runs a **goat dairy** and veg box scheme with her partner, carrying a parlour loan.
She uses **AI every day** for orders and planning and would be disappointed if it were hype.
Her big fear is that AGI hits her **customers' office jobs** before robots reach her farm.
She answers threats with **co-ops** and public money, never going it alone.
Most worried at **two years**, hopeful at five, and focused on a fair handover at ten.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her customers lose their jobs and stop buying before robots come.
whatWouldHelp: **Public money** for farm co-ops to share robots, and income support so town families buy food.
